feed.subtitle: Academic mobility and multilingual teacher education in an AI-mediated world

entry.title: An Ethiopian send-off for 55 new Erasmus Mundus scholars shows how pre-departure support works at scale
entry.summary:
The EU Delegation to Ethiopia announced that 55 Ethiopian students received Erasmus+ scholarships for the 2025-2026 academic year to pursue Erasmus Mundus joint master's degrees across university consortia in 12 European countries. At a pre-departure event on 28 July 2026 at the EU Delegation's office in Addis Ababa, attended by EU Deputy Head of Mission Agnieszka Karpinska and member-state embassy representatives, the new scholars received guidance on travel, visas, and studying and living in Europe, and met other Erasmus Mundus alumni. The Delegation said more than 600 Ethiopian students have received fully funded Erasmus scholarships since 2010.

Why it matters here: This shows the scale Erasmus+ scholarship mobility can reach from a single African country and a practical model for supporting outgoing cohorts, a structured pre-departure briefing on visas, travel and life in Europe, paired with a standing alumni network, that the smaller, bilateral Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project could adapt for its own outgoing master's, doctoral and staff cohorts.

The Brussels Times, 3 August 2026 · News report citing the EU Delegation's own announcement

entry.title: Five Kenyan universities open a managed "academic corridor" to Romania built on Erasmus+ mobility
entry.summary:
Five Kenyan universities, Kabarak, Amref International, Strathmore, Moi and Pwani, signed agreements from 25 to 28 May 2026 with Romania's Danubius International University to open what organisers called East Africa's first fully managed Kenya-Romania academic corridor, facilitated by the Kenyan firm AspiraPath LLC. The corridor offers structured pathways to EU-accredited degrees through joint degree programmes, Erasmus+ mobility frameworks and joint research supervision, letting students complete part of their training locally, and organisers said it aims to reduce the tuition costs, visa difficulties and fragmented partnerships that otherwise limit access to European higher education.

Why it matters here: This is a non-governmental, facilitator-built alternative to a bilateral KA171 project, built explicitly to solve the same access barriers, cost, visas and fragmented links, that Wits-Aix-Marseille's own mobility is designed to address through direct EU funding; it is a useful contrast for the project to watch, since it shows a private, fee-based corridor model competing for the same students a publicly funded exchange like KA171 is meant to serve.

The Standard (Kenya), 25 May 2026 · News report, corroborated by a second Kenyan outlet (The Star)

entry.title: A Nordic study finds European partners kept more say over who joins student-teacher mobility to Africa
entry.summary:
A peer-reviewed study in Nordisk tidsskrift for pedagogikk og kritikk interviewed four facilitators of Norwegian student teachers' mobility in Tanzania and Zambia and three teacher educators in Norway, to examine how (de)colonial dynamics shape this south-bound mobility. It found that facilitators from Norway, the Global North partner, had more freedom to shape mobility activities, including the freedom to choose partner institutions, reproducing asymmetrical power relations through the mobility itself. The authors argue Norwegian teacher education still needs decolonial theoretical frameworks to recognise and address this imbalance.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project moves people in both directions, but this study is a direct warning for any two-way scheme: unless partner choice and activity design are genuinely shared, the European side can end up with more control even when the mobility itself flows south as well as north. It is a check the project's own governance and staff-mobility planning can be measured against.

Massao, P. B. & Bergersen, A., Nordisk tidsskrift for pedagogikk og kritikk, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Brain pain: Nigerian secondary teachers call relocating abroad a right, but say it still hurts
entry.summary:
A phenomenological study in the Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies in Education interviewed 10 Nigerian secondary teachers individually and ran two focus groups of six public and six private school teachers across five states, to understand why many consider leaving the profession or the country. It coins 'brain pain' for the distress of feeling relocation is a personal right while still fearing harm to students, the loss of STEM teachers, and the devaluation of their credentials abroad; family considerations weighed more than fear of visa rejection or starting over. The author argues that retention policy should address professional dignity and moral distress, not salary alone.

Why it matters here: Mobility schemes like Wits-Aix-Marseille's KA171 project move teacher educators and candidates in both directions rather than only outward, but this study is a caution the project can use directly: outward academic mobility, even short-term, touches the same moral and professional terrain as emigration, and support structures should expect ambivalence and guilt alongside enthusiasm, not treat departure as a simple professional-development decision.

Adamu, C. D., Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies in Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: A Ghanaian delegation's Erasmus+ KA171 staff week in Berlin opens talks on joint doctoral training
entry.summary:
A five-member delegation from Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) took part in an Erasmus+ KA171 staff week at Technische Universität Berlin from 22 to 26 June 2026, alongside six other Sub-Saharan African universities. The week combined sessions on the Africa Charter on Transformative Research Collaborations and on equity and funding in international partnerships with a strategic review of the KNUST-TU Berlin link, including a visit to the Einstein Center Digital Future. Follow-up conversations between a KNUST computer scientist and two TU Berlin professors raised the possibility of fully funded PhD training, a joint course in cloud computing and blockchain, and joint research in federated learning and distributed energy systems.

Why it matters here: A staff week used to negotiate concrete joint courses and co-supervised doctoral training, not only to exchange classroom visits, is a model the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project could borrow for its own staff mobility weeks. It also shows KA171 staff mobility being used elsewhere on the continent to open new doctoral pipelines between an African and a European university, the same ambition behind the Wits-Aix-Marseille link.

KNUST International Programmes Office, 22 July 2026 · Institutional news page from the delegation's own international office, not peer-reviewed

entry.title: Wits became a CIVIS strategic partner in Marseille, and a standing Africa-Europe mobility call still runs from it
entry.summary:
On 15 March 2022, at a conference in Marseille co-hosted by the CIVIS Alliance and Aix-Marseille Université, Wits Vice-Chancellor Professor Zeblon Vilakazi signed Wits on as one of six African strategic partner universities, alongside Makerere, Universidade Eduardo Mondlane, and universities in Casablanca, Sfax and Dakar. That status now runs a standing Erasmus+ International Credit Mobility call, open at any time to Wits and CIVIS faculty, postdoctoral and PhD candidates, and staff, funding stays of five days to six months in both directions.

Why it matters here: Wits already holds a formal, funded route into European mobility through CIVIS, distinct from the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project, and Aix-Marseille Université is itself a CIVIS member and the city where Wits signed. The two schemes can run alongside each other: a KA171 staff member unable to find a slot on the bilateral project could use the standing CIVIS call instead, and the CIVIS Hubs are a ready audience for Wits-Aix-Marseille's own findings on bilingual teacher education.

University of the Witwatersrand, March 2022; CIVIS coordinated mobility call, consulted October 2026 · University's own news report of a signing event, supported by the alliance's own published call

entry.title: A Graz medical university secures a worldwide Erasmus+ KA171 grant spanning three South African universities and Makerere
entry.summary:
The Medical University of Graz's International Office secured EUR 326,063.00 in Erasmus+ KA171 funding for a worldwide mobility project running from August 2025 to July 2028, covering incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility for study, traineeships and teaching and training stays. Its partner universities span 12 countries, including three in South Africa (Cape Town, KwaZulu-Natal and Stellenbosch), Makerere University in Uganda, the University of Namibia, and institutions in Australia, Brazil, Chile, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Nepal, Thailand and Ukraine.

Why it matters here: It is a close institutional comparator to the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 grant, showing the scale (over EUR 326,000) and country spread a single global-mobility KA171 project can reach, and a reminder that Wits appears as a partner in other European universities' own KA171 networks, not only as the lead African partner in its own.

Medical University of Graz, International Office, 18 August 2025 · Official university news page, not peer-reviewed

entry.title: A 21-institution Erasmus+ virtual exchange trains African and European students and staff to think critically about AI
entry.summary:
CVEinAI is a 36-month Erasmus+ virtual exchange project, launched in February 2025 and coordinated by the University of Padua, that uses video conferencing, discussion forums and messaging tools to connect students and staff from 21 institutions across 13 countries in Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia, Namibia, Ghana and Botswana. It aims to train 50 higher-education staff in Virtual Exchange design, prepare 100 master's and PhD students as online facilitators, and reach 2,400 students with modules on critical thinking about artificial intelligence, ethical and inclusive AI practice, and intercultural collaboration. A pilot course ran in March and April 2026, and the project has already held an awareness webinar with 77 global participants.

Why it matters here: This is a live, AI-focused Erasmus virtual exchange running at a scale the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 partnership has not yet attempted, and it shows what blended or virtual mobility can add alongside physical exchange for teacher educators, including training a cohort of student facilitators rather than relying only on academic staff. Its spread across 13 countries, nearly half of them in Sub-Saharan Africa, is also a useful comparator for how a smaller, bilateral KA171 project like Wits and Aix-Marseille's might grow its own network.

Critical Virtual Exchange in Artificial Intelligence (CVEinAI), coordinated by the University of Padua with Makerere University's College of Education and External Studies, Erasmus+, 2025 to 2028 · Official project page of the lead implementing partner, not peer-reviewed

entry.title: A Stellenbosch study finds South Africa is becoming a confusing "brain circuity" hub for doctoral students from the rest of Africa, not a clean brain drain or brain circulation
entry.summary:
Using national higher education microdata from 2000 to 2019, researchers at Stellenbosch University's Centre for Research on Evaluation, Science and Technology found that doctoral enrolments from the rest of Africa in South African universities rose from 9 per cent of the total in 2000 to 34 per cent in 2019, before levelling off, with four in ten doctoral students in South Africa in 2019 being international and about one in three of those from elsewhere in Africa. A smaller tracking sample of 463 doctoral graduates from the rest of Africa found 27.5 per cent remained in South Africa, 63.8 per cent returned to their home countries on the continent, and 5.0 per cent moved on to other countries. The authors argue that neither the brain drain nor the brain circulation theory fits cleanly, and coin "brain circuity" for a flow of knowledge marked by indirection and unresolved tension between equity for the rest of Africa and South Africa's own doctoral development targets.

Why it matters here: This is a direct, data-grounded caution for any Africa-Europe mobility scheme that assumes doctoral and staff movement simply flows back to benefit the sending country: the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project and the CIVIS alliance should expect the same mix of return, onward movement and continued stay that this study finds for South Africa itself, rather than a simple two-way exchange.

Van Schalkwyk, F. B., Van Lill, M. H. and Cloete, N., South African Journal of Science, 2021 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: An Erasmus+ Teacher Academy building an AI translation tool for multilingual primary classrooms
entry.summary:
The Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt coordinates the SmartStart Erasmus+ Teacher Academy, a three-year project announced in December 2024 that brings together twelve partner institutions across Germany, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Sweden, Slovakia and Spain with just under 1.5 million euros from the Erasmus+ Teacher Academies initiative. The programme trains teachers and student teachers to use AI-based tools in elementary classrooms through an online course on the eTwinning platform followed by practical work in partner schools, and it is developing a dedicated AI translation tool meant to help integrate children who start school with limited language skills and to let the project's own experts, who speak different languages, exchange expertise.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille mobility already pairs virtual and blended preparation with physical exchange for bilingual teaching students; this consortium's purpose-built AI translation tool, designed to bridge language gaps in multilingual classrooms and among multilingual project staff, is a concrete piece of technology the partnership could test for its own bilingual teacher training.

Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt, news release, 2024 · Institutional news release (Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt)

entry.title: Ten Chinese doctoral students in Malaysia show how South-South mobility can still reproduce Western academic dominance
entry.summary:
Based on qualitative interviews with ten Chinese doctoral students about their perceptions of studying in Malaysia, researchers including Ly Thi Tran at Deakin University examined global South-South student mobility through a decolonization and recolonization framework. They found that students drew real benefits from this alternative route and used it to question Western academic supremacy, but that their own coping strategies and self-perceptions often ended up reinforcing Western dominance rather than displacing it, producing feelings of positivity and inclusion alongside inferiority and anxiety all at once. The authors call for closer attention to the subtler inequalities that persist within mobility routes that bypass the traditional Global South to Global North pattern.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille mobility runs the conventional South-North route that this article contrasts with South-South alternatives; its finding that moving outside the usual route does not automatically escape Western academic hierarchies is a caution for how the partnership frames its own candidates' time in France: success should be judged by what candidates gain, not simply by the fact that they travelled to Europe.

Xu, Tran & Xie, Higher Education, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Higher Education, Springer)

entry.title: What a national dataset of 21,000 Mexican academics shows about who still controls South-North academic mobility
entry.summary:
Drawing on an anonymised national dataset of the 21,257 academics and scientists registered with Mexico's Sistema Nacional de Investigadores and qualified to doctoral level in 2013, researchers based at the Institut de recherche pour le développement and the University of East Anglia found that nearly 40 per cent had obtained part or all of their qualifications abroad. Seventy per cent of those seeking international qualifications went to the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Spain, and to a lesser extent Germany and Canada, countries that have held this top position for four decades, while Latin America took in 6 per cent of the sample with no single country standing out, and Asia, Northern Europe, Oceania and Africa, including South Africa, together attracted only 3 per cent. The authors conclude that these study trajectories, while gradually diversifying, keep consolidating a small number of host countries at the top of the global higher education field.

Why it matters here: This large-scale national dataset is a sobering check on how far one Erasmus+ KA171 partnership can shift an established pattern: it shows that new South-North academic ties, however welcome, tend to keep reinforcing the same handful of dominant destinations, so the Aix-Marseille-Wits project should track whether its own mobility genuinely widens Wits candidates' options or simply adds one more well-trodden route to Europe.

Gérard & Lebeau, International Journal of Educational Development, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article (International Journal of Educational Development), open access

entry.title: Twenty-one Italian universities, seventy-eight African partners: Brescia's recovery-funded doctoral and staff mobility scheme
entry.summary:
The Università degli Studi di Brescia coordinates TNE UNITAFRICA, a transnational education scheme joining 21 Italian universities, through the Coordinamento Universitario per la Cooperazione allo Sviluppo, with 78 partner institutions across Africa, funded through Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan rather than Erasmus+. Its 2025 call funded three doctoral mobilities of two months each and three staff teaching mobilities of eight days each, to be hosted at one of ten named partner universities in Senegal, Ghana, Kenya, Tanzania, Somalia and Mozambique, in agriculture, architecture, engineering and global health.

Why it matters here: A national recovery fund, rather than Erasmus+, paying for short, tightly scoped doctoral and staff mobilities to a fixed list of named partner universities is a workable alternative funding model and administrative shape the Aix-Marseille-Wits project can point to if Erasmus+ KA171 funding for this partnership is ever interrupted or needs a smaller, faster-to-run complement.

Università degli Studi di Brescia, international mobility notice, 2025 · Institutional notice (Università degli Studi di Brescia)

entry.title: Nine in ten staff say their professional network grew, but two in three call their institution's recognition merely "informal"
entry.summary:
France's national Erasmus+ agency tracked 7,142 staff members, 42% of them from higher education, who took part in Erasmus+ mobility in 2016/17, through participant feedback and a follow-up survey sent eighteen months after their mobility ended. Ninety-one per cent said the experience had boosted or strengthened their professional network, half said they had actively or moderately changed their professional practice as a result, and two-thirds said their institution had recognised the value of their mobility, but mostly only informally rather than through any formal process.

Why it matters here: The gap this report finds between personal gains and institutional recognition is exactly the risk for the Aix-Marseille-Wits exchange: unless returning staff and academics have a formal route, a seminar series, a curriculum review, a credited role, to carry what they learned back into the Wits School of Education's own teaching, the mobility risks staying a personal benefit rather than becoming an institutional one.

Agence Erasmus+ France / Éducation Formation, The Erasmus+ Observatory, Notes No. 12, 2025 · National agency evaluation report (Agence Erasmus+ France / Éducation Formation), survey-based

entry.title: Six warnings for virtual exchange as it moves from language classrooms to the Global South
entry.summary:
A University of León researcher traces how virtual exchange has grown from early bilingual North-North language partnerships into North-South collaborations and partnerships with conflict zones, and sets out six concerns for practitioners: structural inequalities in project design that risk reproducing Global North dominance, communication barriers in lingua franca exchanges that favour already-privileged learners, psychological risks for students paired with conflict-zone partners, political and institutional pressure around controversial partnerships, the gap between genuine social impact and tokenistic engagement, and keeping motivated an increasingly well-travelled student population. The author calls for virtual exchange programmes that address power imbalances directly, give stronger linguistic scaffolding and use trauma-informed protocols rather than treating any cross-border contact as automatically beneficial.

Why it matters here: Erasmus+ KA171 moves people rather than running virtual exchanges, but the Aix-Marseille-Wits mobility runs alongside blended and virtual preparation in both directions; this is a direct checklist against which to test whether the project's own design, who sets the agenda, whose language dominates, what happens to the partnership if either side's politics shift, avoids reproducing the imbalance the article warns against.

O'Dowd, Language Learning & Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Language Learning & Technology), open access

entry.title: Teach4Sustainability: an Erasmus+ virtual exchange links student teachers in four African countries with peers in Germany and Spain
entry.summary:
Teach4Sustainability is an Erasmus+ Virtual Exchange project of 36 months, running from February 2026 to January 2029, that connects student teachers, teacher educators and institutions in Germany, Spain, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Rwanda and The Gambia to strengthen climate change and sustainability education in teacher training. Coordinated by Universität Münster, it works through small intercultural groups, real-time and flexible online interaction and problem-based learning, in formats designed to be mobile-friendly and accessible in low-bandwidth settings. The consortium held its first virtual kick-off meeting in February 2026 and launched a multi-country needs assessment in April 2026.

Why it matters here: Not every Wits or Aix-Marseille student teacher will travel, so this is a ready model for the virtual side of the KA171 exchange: structured online work between African and European student teachers on sustainable development, one of the joint themes named in the project. Its design for phones and low bandwidth is a practical lesson for any joint sessions that include Wits School of Education students.

Institut für Didaktik der Geographie, Universität Münster, project page, 2026 · Official project page of the coordinating university (Universität Münster), for a project funded under the Erasmus+ Virtual Exchanges call for Sub-Saharan Africa (ERASMUS-EDU-2025-VIRT-EXCH-SSA, project 101251923); partners and dates also confirmed on the UNED project page and in Münster's launch notice of 30 January 2026

entry.title: Why Ghanaian graduates of European universities go home or stay: 45 interviews on the return decision
entry.summary:
Researchers at Charles University interviewed 45 Ghanaians who had graduated from European universities: 22 returnees interviewed in Ghana and 23 non-returnees interviewed abroad. Combining the Theory of Planned Behaviour with migration concepts, they found that return intentions often shift over time and that the decision is rarely driven by a single factor, but by an interplay of structural constraints, personal motivations and normative pressures. Participants expressed both pro-return and pro-stay orientations, yet perceived family expectations tended to favour staying abroad.

Why it matters here: KA171 stays are short and return is built in, but this study shows that intentions to stay can grow after a European experience, so the Wits School of Education should plan how returning master's and doctoral candidates are drawn back into its work rather than assume it. It also gives the project a frame for asking what the sending institution gains from the exchange with Aix-Marseille, not only how many people travel.

Yeboah, M., & Novotný, J., International Journal of Educational Development, 2025 · Peer-reviewed article, International Journal of Educational Development (Elsevier), a qualitative interview study by researchers at Charles University

entry.title: Four universities in Finland and Mozambique co-create teacher education modules and train 912 educators and teachers
entry.summary:
The TEPATE project, run from 2020 to 2024 and funded by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Finland, joined the Pedagogical University of Maputo and ISET One World in Mozambique with Jamk University of Applied Sciences and the University of Lapland to improve the balance between theory and practice in Mozambican teacher education. Across the 4 universities, 36 teacher educators developed 3 modules for teacher education, 276 student teachers piloted them, and 912 teacher educators, secondary school teachers and school managers were trained on their content. The project lists weak multilingualism pedagogies among the problems facing the teaching profession that it set out to address.

Why it matters here: This is a worked model of what the Wits and Aix-Marseille partnership can aim for beyond individual trips: teacher educators from both sides co-creating modules, piloting them with student teachers and carrying them into schools. Its attention to multilingualism pedagogies speaks directly to the bilingual teaching master's at the heart of the exchange with INSPE.

Jamk University of Applied Sciences news, 2024 · University news article, institutional source (Jamk University of Applied Sciences, a project partner), reporting the results of a project funded by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Finland

entry.title: An Erasmus+ project trains 40 lecturers across five African countries to lead teacher education for sustainable development
entry.summary:
Leuphana Universität Lüneburg leads an Erasmus+ capacity-building project on teacher leadership for education for sustainable development, working with universities in South Africa, Zambia, Namibia, Malawi and Kenya alongside partners in Germany, Cyprus and Greece. By May 2026 the project had completed a Training of Trainers programme producing 40 trained lecturers able to teach education for sustainable development leadership courses and guide colleagues in running education for sustainable development change projects. The University of the Witwatersrand leads the scaling of these change projects jointly with the University of Malawi.

Why it matters here: The University of the Witwatersrand already runs an international Erasmus+ consortium role here, leading change-project scaling jointly with the University of Malawi, so the Wits School of Education can draw directly on its own cascade model, the Training of Trainers approach that turned 40 lecturers into in-house trainers, when preparing staff and candidates for the Aix-Marseille exchange.

Hülsmann, M., Leuphana Universität Lüneburg news, 2026 · University news article, institutional source (Leuphana Universität Lüneburg), reporting on an active Erasmus+-funded capacity-building project

entry.title: Aix-Marseille's own teacher-training institute launches a plurilingualism-and-AI exchange with Dakar's teacher training centre
entry.summary:
Aix-Marseille Université's INSPE and the Centre Régional de Formation des Personnels de l'Éducation (CRFPE) of Dakar launched a teaching and teacher-training cooperation project on 14 November 2025, supported by the French Embassy in Senegal. The launch set up two collaborative workspaces in Senegal, one on plurilingualism and artificial intelligence and one on fablab and artificial intelligence, to share experiences and co-construct teaching resources suited to local contexts. In March 2026 ten student teachers from the Dakar CRFPE are due to visit the Aix-Marseille INSPE to take courses and meet primary school pupils.

Why it matters here: Aix-Marseille's INSPE is the lead partner in the Erasmus+ KA171-HED project with Wits, and this Dakar exchange shows the same institute already running a bilingual, AI-themed teacher-training partnership with a Global South partner, a tested workspace format and a direct institutional contact for lessons on plurilingual content and for twinning the Wits mobility cohorts with a comparable Francophone West African partner.

Aix-Marseille Université, INSPE · Institutional programme page, Aix-Marseille Université INSPE (official partner institution), reporting the project's launch

entry.title: Parma's Erasmus+ KA171-HED fund gives extreme priority to the most disadvantaged staff and students from Rwanda, Senegal and Niger
entry.summary:
The University of Parma's Centre for International University Cooperation (CUCI) was awarded an Erasmus+ KA171-HED fund supporting academic mobility with universities in Rwanda, Senegal and Niger. The fund covers 21 incoming teaching-staff positions, who take three-week laboratory training courses and summer schools updating pedagogical methods, and 19 incoming student places for three to four month internships. Selection explicitly requires gender balance and gives extreme priority to the most economically disadvantaged students and teaching staff from the partner countries.

Why it matters here: This KA171-HED consortium shows a concrete, publicly stated equity rule, explicit gender balance and extreme priority for the most disadvantaged applicants, for selecting incoming teaching staff and structuring their pedagogical training, a model the Wits and Aix-Marseille partnership could adapt when it sets its own selection criteria for master's, doctoral and staff mobility cohorts.

Università di Parma (CUCI) · Institutional announcement page, Università di Parma (official recipient institution of the Erasmus+ KA171-HED award)

entry.title: Moroccan researchers argue for virtual exchange built into English teacher education, not as a stand-in for travel
entry.summary:
This paper by researchers at Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdellah University in Fes and Mohammed First University in Oujda examines virtual exchange as a practical form of internationalisation at home in Moroccan teacher education for teachers of English as a foreign language. Drawing on a narrative review of research on internationalisation, virtual exchange and intercultural learning, it argues that virtual exchange is not a simple digital substitute for physical mobility but a structured, guided and reflective pedagogy. It proposes a pathway in which virtual exchange embedded in the curriculum puts internationalisation at home into practice and creates conditions for future teachers to develop intercultural literacy.

Why it matters here: Only some Wits School of Education and INSPE Aix-Marseille students and staff will travel under the grant, and this North African case for embedding virtual exchange in the teacher education curriculum suggests how the partnership could reach the rest, for instance through shared online modules on multilingual teaching before and after each physical stay. Being conceptual, it offers a design to test rather than measured outcomes.

Abdellaoui and Zerrik, Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies in Education, 15(6), 129-150, 2026 · Journal article, open access (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); a conceptual paper based on a narrative literature review

entry.title: A Swiss teacher education department sends trainee teachers on two-month placements in Kenya, Togo and Ghana
entry.summary:
Since 2011 the Department of Education and Learning and University of Teacher Education (DFA/ASP) of SUPSI in Switzerland has run a mobility programme that places trainee teachers in schools and other educational settings abroad for two months; relaunched in 2022/23 as "Experiencing school elsewhere", its 2024-2025 destinations included Costa Rica, Kenya, Togo and Ghana. The module combines a preparatory phase on intercultural skills and comparative school systems, a field phase accompanied by local professionals, and a concluding phase assessed through an interview and a multimedia product; 44 participants had taken part between 2011 and June 2025. Most described the experience as transformative, while the difficulties they reported included the emotional impact of profound social inequalities, unforeseen events and misunderstandings over communication habits.

Why it matters here: This is a working model of short, structured placements for student teachers in African schools, with preparation, local mentoring and assessed reflection, which the Wits School of Education and INSPE Aix-Marseille could adapt for master's students in bilingual teaching. Its candid list of difficulties, from the emotional weight of inequality to misread communication codes, is a useful checklist for preparing students who will move in both directions between South Africa and France.

SUPSI Newsroom, 23 June 2025 · University newsroom article (interview with the programme coordinator)

entry.title: Spanish bilingual student teachers who took part in international programmes rate their intercultural and plurilingual competence higher
entry.summary:
A questionnaire survey of 99 bilingual pre-service teachers at four public universities in Spain measured their self-perceived intercultural and plurilingual competences against gender, schooling in a bilingual primary track, participation in international programmes and language proficiency. Mann-Whitney U tests indicated that both competences seem linked to participation in international programmes and to language proficiency, while bilingual primary schooling had a weak effect and no gender differences were found. The two competences were positively correlated.

Why it matters here: The project's master's mobility is for students in bilingual teaching, and this study links international programme participation to bilingual student teachers' view of their own intercultural and plurilingual competence, which suggests what the Wits School of Education and INSPE Aix-Marseille could measure before and after each exchange. As a self-report survey with no follow-up over time, it shows an association rather than proof that mobility causes the gain.

Arnaiz-Castro, Gómez-Parra and Espejo, Revista Interuniversitaria de Formación del Profesorado, 99(38.3), 63-84, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 ES)

entry.title: Greek university's 2026 Erasmus+ KA171 call results add a first South African partner
entry.summary:
In its August 2026 call results announcement, Hellenic Mediterranean University reported an Erasmus+ KA171 grant of 247,577 euros (agreement 2026-1-EL01-KA171-HED-000442730) funding 66 mobility places across 68 partner universities in 22 countries, made up of 42 staff and 24 student mobilities. The 2026 round added twelve new partner institutions, including, for the first time, South Africa's Durban University of Technology, alongside institutions in the Western Balkans, the Mediterranean region and the Neighbourhood East.

Why it matters here: As a European KA171 grant holder running the same European Commission funding instrument as the Wits-Aix-Marseille project, Hellenic Mediterranean University's published figures give the administrative staff coordinating the Wits-Aix-Marseille exchange a useful benchmark of typical grant size and mobility numbers.

Hellenic Mediterranean University International Relations Office, 2026 · University international relations office programme page

entry.title: South Africa to Uganda benchmarking visit on teacher assessment and curriculum reform
entry.summary:
In July 2026 a delegation of 24 officials from Uganda's Ministry of Education and Sports visited Tshwane University of Technology's Soshanguve South campus in South Africa to benchmark teacher assessment and curriculum reform practices. The visit focused on formative and summative assessment approaches for competency-based education, and Tshwane University of Technology was noted as one of only a few institutions on the continent offering a comprehensive four-year assessment programme for student teachers. The two sides discussed establishing a memorandum of understanding on teacher education and inclusive education reform.

Why it matters here: This shows a comparable model of staff benchmarking and curriculum and assessment exchange in teacher education, from which the Wits School of Education's Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille's INSPE can draw lessons, particularly for the administrative staff who will organise joint training visits.

Tshwane University of Technology newsroom, 2026 · University newsroom article

entry.title: CIVIS seed funding scheme for joint African-European research, linking Wits and Aix-Marseille directly
entry.summary:
CIVIS, the European University Alliance of eleven European and six African universities including Aix-Marseille University and the University of the Witwatersrand, ran a seed funding call for African-European research collaborations that opened on 25 March 2025 and closed on 31 May 2025, covering activities such as doctoral schools, workshops and joint grant-writing visits. Each selected project could receive up to 10,000 euros, with staff mobility costs covered up to 850 euros within Europe and 1,500 euros between Europe and Africa, and funded projects had to be completed by 30 June 2026.

Why it matters here: This CIVIS seed funding scheme directly links Aix-Marseille University and the University of the Witwatersrand as fellow alliance members, giving Wits School of Education and Wits International a concrete, existing funding route to extend the Erasmus+ mobility into joint doctoral schools and research visits with Aix-Marseille beyond the KA171 grant itself.

CIVIS European University Alliance call page, 2025 · European University Alliance funding call page

entry.title: Teaching mathematics, science and technology in the mother tongue across Africa: a Wits scoping review
entry.summary:
Two Wits School of Education researchers reviewed research published between 2014 and 2025 on mother tongue-based bilingual education in primary mathematics, science and technology across Africa and found 45 outputs that met their criteria, with marked growth in the last six years and a heavy concentration in South Africa. Translanguaging and teacher preparation were the dominant themes, and no research was found on bilingual education in technology education. The authors conclude that the approach works only if teacher preparation is strengthened and classroom practice is brought into line with language-in-education policy.

Why it matters here: The project's master's mobility is for students in bilingual teaching, and this review, written in the Wits School of Education, maps what African research already says on the subject. It gives Wits and INSPE Aix-Marseille a shared starting reading list and points to gaps, such as technology education, that joint work on multilingualism could fill.

Hamukwaya and Essien, South African Journal of Childhood Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Can Erasmus+ mobility change a teacher? A close study of two teachers in the Netherlands
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Universidade de Lisboa and Leiden University ran a multiple case study of two teachers in the Netherlands who took part in Erasmus+ Key Action 1 mobility for professional development, using interviews, biographical narratives and focus groups. Mobility prompted deep pedagogical reflection and a rethinking of the teachers' European identity, and the participants linked their personal and professional growth. The authors warn that such mobility succeeds as professional development only when it becomes part of a school-wide improvement strategy rather than an isolated trip.

Why it matters here: The project sends academics and administrative staff as well as students, and this study's warning applies to the Wits School of Education as a sending institution: plan from the start how each returning participant's learning will be shared with colleagues and built into programmes. With only two teachers, it offers ideas to test rather than evidence at scale.

Martins, Alves, Tinoca and Mearns, European Educational Research Journal, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: What a three-year KA171 project between Venice and Stellenbosch delivered
entry.summary:
The Venice International University Erasmus+ Mobility Consortium, formed with its Italian member universities, ran a KA171 project with Stellenbosch University from 2022 to 2025 covering long-term and blended student mobility, short doctoral exchanges, and staff teaching and training. Its report records 6 Stellenbosch students on a blended summer session in August 2024 and 3 on a full semester, 16 student and 8 staff mobilities in intensive graduate activities, doctoral exchanges in both directions including one under joint supervision, and administrative staff from each side attending the other's training. Participant surveys gave a weighted average of 88% for students' skills and personal development and 92% for staff's professional skills and growth.

Why it matters here: A South African KA171 partnership that has run its full course, with the same strands as the Wits and Aix-Marseille project: doctoral exchange with joint supervision, staff training for administrators and blended short mobility. Its report shows the modest numbers such projects realistically move and the survey measures a final report uses, a ready template for planning and reporting.

Venice International University, Erasmus+ project report (undated page; activities to July 2025) · Institutional final project report; results self-reported from participant surveys

entry.title: Twenty-eight institutions across Africa and Europe join forces to fix the teacher shortage
entry.summary:
The Regional Teachers Initiative for Africa, a 100 million euro European Union programme running from 2024 to 2030 and coordinated by the Finnish National Agency for Education, has launched six research projects (running May 2025 to November 2026) bringing together 28 universities, NGOs and other education institutions from 12 African countries and 6 European countries. The projects work on teacher wellbeing and retention, professional development at scale, early number learning and professional learning communities, with the aim of reducing teacher shortages and attrition and improving teacher motivation.

Why it matters here: This shows a cross-continental teacher-education research consortium built at a scale well beyond a single bilateral exchange, and a working model of how funders now expect joint research and capacity-building outputs, not only mobility, from Africa-Europe education partnerships. It is a useful comparator, and a possible dissemination partner, for the Wits and Aix-Marseille academics working jointly on multilingualism and sustainable development.

Finnish National Agency for Education (EDUFI), Regional Teachers Initiative for Africa, 2025 · Institutional news page of a national education agency coordinating an EU-funded programme

entry.title: Why African visa rules still carry a colonial charge, a German policy institute argues
entry.summary:
A briefing from the German institute Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik argues that European visa rules for African applicants still carry colonial-era inequality: it reports that African applicants to Schengen countries faced roughly a 30 per cent rejection rate in 2022 against a 17.5 per cent global average, that the European Union collected about 130 million euros in fees from rejected African applications in 2023, and that African legal migration to Europe fell from roughly 400,000 to 500,000 a year before 2012 to about 270,000 to 290,000 more recently. It illustrates the asymmetry with a Kenya-Germany labour agreement and the fact that Germans can travel to Namibia without a visa while Tanzanians must pay 83 euros and supply extensive documentation.

Why it matters here: For a project designed to move people in both directions between Wits and Aix-Marseille, this is a sober reminder that visa access, not grant funding, is often the real limit on genuine reciprocal mobility, and that the underlying inequality runs one way. It is useful evidence to raise early with the partners' international offices when planning the South to North legs of the exchange.

Franzisca Zanker, Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik, Mobility, Trust and Agency Spotlight 45, 2025 · Policy analysis from SWP, the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, which advises the Bundestag and German government

entry.title: A Mexican university's answer to funding cuts: send students online instead
entry.summary:
An ethnographic study from Universidad Juarez Autonoma de Tabasco in Mexico describes a virtual exchange pilot run in the first semester of 2024 that paired Mexican students with peers in Greece and Japan, adopted after sustained budget cuts had limited the university's traditional mobility and exchange programmes. Using participant observation of written, image and video contributions, the authors conclude that curriculum internationalisation remained achievable with the resources available, giving students meaningful contact with peers from other cultures without the cost of travel.

Why it matters here: This is a direct account of a Global South institution turning to virtual exchange specifically because funding for physical mobility had been cut, the same budget pressure that limits how many Wits and Aix-Marseille staff and students the Erasmus+ grant can send each year. It offers a concrete, low-cost pilot design that the two schools could adapt for students and staff who miss out on funded places.

Cuevas Álvarez, Pérez Mendoza, Vélez Tellez, Zetina Pérez, Coeto Calcáneo and Alfaro García, Journal of International Students, Vol 15(1), 2025 · Peer-reviewed open-access journal article, Journal of International Students

entry.title: A six-university Erasmus+ network trains careers and start-up staff across Africa and Europe
entry.summary:
In May 2026 the University of Ghana announced it had joined a 2026 to 2028 Erasmus+ project led by the University of Münster in Germany, together with Ashesi University, United States International University-Africa (Kenya), Kepler College (Rwanda) and the American University in Cairo (Egypt), to strengthen career development, entrepreneurship training and intercultural learning across Africa and Europe. The project runs staff exchanges, institutional visits, online seminars, workshops and training on start-up development and labour market engagement, coordinated at the University of Ghana by its Careers and Counselling Services Directorate and Innovation Unit. It will also support research into country-specific market opportunities for student-led start-ups.

Why it matters here: This is a live example of a multi-country Erasmus+ staff-exchange network built around a specific professional function, careers and start-up support, rather than a single discipline, a structure the Wits-Aix-Marseille administrative staff mobility strand could borrow directly when designing exchanges for the staff who run the mobility programme itself and its CIVIS link.

University of Ghana, May 2026 · Institutional news page, University of Ghana

entry.title: A continent-wide, geolocated map of nine years of Erasmus+ student exchanges
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Helsinki built a geolocated dataset of about 2.3 million Erasmus+ students and 2.2 million individual mobility movements across Europe between 2014 and 2022, geocoded to local and regional units with over 96 per cent accuracy. The data show large cities such as Vienna, Berlin and Madrid keeping a stable balance of incoming and outgoing students, smaller cities fluctuating more, and mobility dropping sharply in 2020 before recovering toward pre-pandemic levels. Regions across Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy and much of Northern Europe emerge as hotspots of diverse student interaction.

Why it matters here: This gives the Wits-Aix-Marseille project a rigorous methodology and a scale benchmark for tracking and evaluating its own mobility flows over its 36 months, and a reminder that even a well-funded scheme like Erasmus+ shows uneven, city-by-city patterns and a sharp shock from external disruption that a small bilateral exchange should plan for.

Väisänen, T., Malekzadeh, M., Inkeröinen, O. and Järv, O., Scientific Data, 2025 · Peer-reviewed open-access dataset article, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International

entry.title: A Tanzanian open university's struggle to reach non-mobile international students at a distance
entry.summary:
Drawing on interviews with staff at an open and distance-learning university in Tanzania, this article examines how internationalisation at a distance lets non-mobile international students engage with courses without leaving home, at a time when Tanzania positions itself as an expanding international higher education destination. Using the capabilities approach and ideas of conversion factors and third space, the authors identify infrastructure gaps, including unreliable ICT and a shortage of staff with the right skills, as central barriers. They argue that institutions should pool resources and act as a community rather than alone if virtual mobility is to support the SDG 4 goal of broader access.

Why it matters here: This is close evidence on virtual and blended mobility from within the Global South, useful as a comparison for the parts of the Wits-Aix-Marseille exchange that could run online, and as a caution that ICT infrastructure and staff readiness, not just funding, determine whether distance mobility actually reaches students who cannot travel.

Ngalomba, S., Mkwananzi, F. and Mukwambo, P., British Journal of Educational Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (British Journal of Educational Technology, vol. 56, issue 2), hybrid open access under CC BY-NC 4.0, verified via the University of Glasgow institutional repository record

entry.title: A report puts a price on Africa's outbound students and asks who gains
entry.summary:
This report frames outbound African student mobility as a continental economic question rather than an individual opportunity. It states that more than 460,000 African students leave the continent each year for higher education abroad, at an estimated annual loss of 2.5 billion United States dollars in tuition, innovation and forgone opportunity, and that while 54 per cent of those students are scholarship funded only 18 per cent return. It argues that African countries together spend more on overseas tuition than 25 countries spend on their entire education budgets, and estimates a 500 million dollar annual reinvestment if a quarter of mobile students stayed through hybrid programmes.

Why it matters here: The Wits and Aix-Marseille project sends people out and brings people in, and this is the sharpest available statement of the risk on the outbound side, that mobility can shade into permanent departure. Reading it alongside the project's design is a way of asking what keeps a returning candidate in place, and its figures are a useful counterweight to the celebratory register of most mobility reporting, though they come from a private research group rather than a peer-reviewed source.

Ekanem, K., African Student Mobility Report 2025, Mo-Research Strategy Group, published on Zenodo · Independent research report, openly available on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, not peer reviewed

entry.title: An Erasmus Mundus master on education, migration and diversity keeps multilingualism as a core module
entry.summary:
EDU_MIG is an Erasmus Mundus master in Education, Migration and Diversity that began taking students in 2025, coordinated by the University of Education Schwäbisch Gmünd with the University of Gävle and the University of Calabria. It offers 25 places a year, a majority of them carrying Erasmus Mundus scholarships that cover tuition, health insurance and a monthly allowance, over two years with mobility between the partner countries. The curriculum is built on three core strands, Migration and Interculturality, Multilingualism, and Educational Sciences, and the network of academic and professional partners runs across Germany, Sweden, Italy, Türkiye and Benin, where students can take internships.

Why it matters here: The Wits and Aix-Marseille project moves master's students in bilingual teaching and academics working on multilingualism, and this is a fully built European programme with multilingualism as a named module and an African partner already inside the consortium. It is worth reading both as a curriculum model for the bilingual teaching strand and as a possible route by which a Wits colleague could join a Mundus consortium later.

EDU_MIG consortium, programme website, first cohort from 2025 · Official programme website of a consortium funded by the European Union under Erasmus Mundus

entry.title: Two hundred and fifty mobilities between Britain, Uganda and Kenya, and a survey to find out what they were worth
entry.summary:
Nottingham Trent University reports that its Erasmus+ International Credit Mobility programme ran in two phases, 2018 to 2021 and 2021 to 2023, and enabled over 250 transnational mobilities between the United Kingdom, Uganda and Kenya. The first phase paired NTU with Makerere University in public health for research development, capacity building and knowledge exchange among staff and undergraduate, master's and doctoral students; the second widened to nursing, microbiology and environmental sciences, and to Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology and Mount Kenya University on a 36 month grant of 136,360 euros. Participants took part in research training, writing retreats, summer schools and conference presentations, and the university has since run an ethics-approved survey of NTU and Makerere participants to assess what the mobilities changed.

Why it matters here: This is the nearest completed model of what the Wits and Aix-Marseille project is starting: a multi-year, two-direction partnership between a European and African university running across degree levels and staff. The detail worth borrowing is the evaluation, an ethics-approved survey of participants after the fact, which is exactly the evidence a 36 month project should be gathering from its first cohort rather than at the end.

Nottingham Trent University, Eastern Africa Centre project page, updated July 2024 · Project page of the host university, naming partners, funding and leads

entry.title: Wits signs the CIVIS Africa Charter and confirms its first Erasmus Mundus joint master's bid at the Casablanca forum
entry.summary:
At the first African-European CIVIS Forum for Research and Education, held in Casablanca, Morocco, from 25 to 27 March 2026, the University of the Witwatersrand signed the Africa Charter for Transformative Research Collaborations, which sets out ten principles on power imbalances in global knowledge production and six policy aspirations for institutional change. Wits also confirmed it will lead its first African application to the European Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's programme, on polycrisis studies, and reported CIVIS staff and student mobility already running through its TRACEE master's programme and Blended Intensive Programmes.

Why it matters here: This project's own academic lead at Wits, Professor Emmanuel Ojo, is named in the same report as co-developing a CIVIS doctoral micro-credential on artificial intelligence and research with partner universities in Madrid, Rome, Athens and Glasgow, showing an existing staff mobility channel and a joint credentialing model the Aix-Marseille partnership can draw on, while the Africa Charter's principles on power imbalance are a direct check for the project's own design.

University of the Witwatersrand, September 2026 · Institutional news article, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: A Southeast Asian policy brief sets out how ten countries could build a shared framework for teacher exchange and mutual recognition
entry.summary:
A 2025 policy brief from the ASEAN Secretariat, written by a researcher at the University of the Philippines and based on focus groups and key informant interviews, found that Southeast Asian nations have used mutual recognition arrangements since 2005 in seven professional sectors, from engineering to accountancy, but never for teaching. It reported that about a quarter of pre-primary teachers and almost a tenth of primary teachers in the region lacked nationally recognised qualifications, and it recommended an ASEAN teacher exchange scheme, a regional coordination body, and visa, language and short-term training support for mobile teachers.

Why it matters here: A comparative case from outside Europe: its focus on mutual recognition of qualifications and on visa, language and pre-departure training support for mobile teachers names the same practical hurdles that the Wits and Aix-Marseille project must plan for as it moves students and staff between two different national qualification systems, and its call for a dedicated regional coordination body is a model the project's own administrative strand could test.

Dr Ethel Agnes Pascua-Valenzuela, ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community Policy Brief No. 22, 2025 · Intergovernmental policy brief, ASEAN Secretariat, open access

entry.title: A scoping review of virtual exchange research in teacher education finds outcomes depend on educator effort and institutional backing
entry.summary:
A scoping review by researchers at the University of Education Freiburg, published in the Center for Educational Policy Studies Journal in March 2025, examined research published between 2020 and 2023 on virtual exchange in teacher education, covering how such exchanges are planned, implemented and evaluated. It found virtual exchange to be a multifaceted field with multiple aims and impacts whose success depends heavily on educator effort, institutional support and student participation, and called for future research to move beyond language teacher education and to combine different study scales.

Why it matters here: Evidence and a ready-made literature map for the project's virtual and blended mobility strand: it can guide how the Wits and Aix-Marseille partnership designs, resources and evaluates any online or blended components alongside physical exchange, and its finding that outcomes hinge on institutional support is a direct planning point for both partners.

Claudia Ingrisch-Rupp and Vasileios Symeonidis, Center for Educational Policy Studies Journal, Vol. 15 No. 1, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: South Africa in Erasmus+: 2,746 outbound and 1,879 inbound mobilities in the last programme, and 600 more student places to Europe from the 2022 selections
entry.summary:
The DHET's international scholarships portal records South Africa's participation in Erasmus+ since 2014 across all the components open to partner countries. Under the 2014 to 2020 programme, International Credit Mobility took 2,746 students and staff from South Africa to Europe and brought 1,879 from Europe to South Africa; 78 South African students won full Erasmus Mundus Joint Master scholarships, 29 capacity-building projects ran with four coordinated by South African institutions, and six Jean Monnet projects and one network were implemented. From the 2022 selections of the 2021 to 2027 programme, the page lists 461 staff mobilities to Europe and 416 from Europe to South Africa, 600 student mobilities to Europe and 128 into South Africa, three new capacity-building projects, ten instances of TVET capacity-building participation and five instances in two virtual exchange projects.

Why it matters here: The national picture into which the Aix-Marseille partnership fits: these figures show that the Wits mobilities are part of an established South African flow with a home department that tracks it, which matters for reporting, for Wits International's dealings with DHET, and for arguing that teacher education deserves a larger share.

Department of Higher Education and Training, International Scholarships portal, Erasmus+ Programme page (consulted 18 September 2026) · Official page of a national government department

entry.title: What the partner already runs: INSPE Aix-Marseille's student mobility page, from Erasmus+ semesters to CIVIS schools and teaching placements abroad
entry.summary:
The Institute of Teaching and Education (INSPE) at Aix-Marseille Université sets out the mobility routes open to its trainee teachers. Erasmus+ study periods last from three to twelve months per study cycle at eleven partner universities in Germany, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, Greece, the Netherlands and Switzerland, with credits validated on return; CIVIS supports study visits to alliance partners, and CIVIS schools offer one- to three-week intensive courses with practical work. Short formats include the International Education Week summer school at Tübingen, taught in English, and a Franco-German musical education exchange with Universität Hamburg. Placement mobility covers Erasmus+ teaching internships of two to twelve months and France Éducation International language-assistant posts of four to twelve months, with grants arranged through the international mobility manager.

Why it matters here: This is the machinery the Wits School of Education will plug into: INSPE already sends and receives trainee teachers on semester exchanges and short CIVIS formats, so the KA171 mobilities can copy its credit validation, its short-course model and its mobility-manager role rather than inventing them.

INSPE Aix-Marseille, International, Student mobility page (consulted 18 September 2026) · Official page of the partner institution

entry.title: Fifty-five educators on what Erasmus staff exchange did for them: leadership, intercultural competence and the barriers that keep others at home
entry.summary:
A qualitative study at Transylvania University of Brașov drew on in-depth interviews with 55 educators from European and non-European countries who had taken part in Erasmus staff exchange, tracing how short-term mobility reshaped their professional practice, career paths and engagement with their institutions. Participants reported gains in intercultural competence, global awareness and pedagogical innovation, and described a renewed sense of purpose and an expanded leadership identity on return. The authors also record persistent barriers, including financial constraints, gaps in language proficiency and uneven institutional support, and argue that unless these are addressed Erasmus will serve the already advantaged rather than transform education systems.

Why it matters here: Evidence for the staff strand of the Wits and Aix-Marseille project: it suggests what to ask returning academics and administrators in the project's own evaluation, and its warning about language and institutional support speaks directly to a partnership working across English and French.

Ivasciuc, Marinescu and Ispas, Education Sciences, volume 15, issue 6, article 712, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY)

entry.title: How Erasmus+ KA171 mobility works: the rules this project runs under
entry.summary:
The Erasmus+ Programme Guide sets the rules for mobility projects for higher education students and staff. Projects supported by external policy funds, the strand this partnership falls under, run for 24 or 36 months, cover every study cycle from short cycle to doctoral, and allow blended mobility that combines a physical stay with a virtual component. Regional rules apply: for Sub-Saharan Africa at least 35% of the budget must go to mobility with the region's least developed countries and no more than 8% to any single country. Partner institutions outside the Programme countries cannot sign the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education but must respect its principles, so fair and transparent selection, recognition of learning outcomes and support for participants have to be made explicit in the inter-institutional agreement.

Why it matters here: The rulebook for this project: the 36-month duration, the doctoral and blended mobility options, and the requirement that selection and recognition be spelt out in the inter-institutional agreement all come from here, which is why the Wits side's first task is that agreement.

European Commission, Erasmus+ Programme Guide, Part B, Key Action 1, mobility projects for higher education students and staff (version consulted 16 September 2026) · Official programme guide of the European Commission

entry.title: CIVIS asks Europe to treat academic mobility from Africa as a visa priority
entry.summary:
CIVIS, the European University Alliance to which Aix-Marseille University belongs and which has African member institutions, has published a position paper on visas for Africa-Europe academic mobility. Drawing on its own surveys, it reports that African applicants face long waiting times, difficulty getting appointments, high costs, long journeys to consulates and heavy documentation, which lead to delayed or cancelled exchanges. It welcomes the European Commission's moves to modernise visa policy and asks for three additions: academic mobility as a priority category with longer-validity, multiple-entry visas; simplified procedures extended to short academic stays such as conferences and research visits; and strategic priority for Africa, with more consular capacity and faster processing.

Why it matters here: The practical risk this project must plan for: a Wits student or colleague holding an Erasmus+ grant still needs a French visa in time, so nomination windows and consulate lead times belong in the mobility calendar from the start, and the CIVIS position gives the partnership a policy argument to cite.

CIVIS position paper and newsroom, 9 September 2026 · Position paper of a European University Alliance, drawing on its own member surveys
